answers.question: What is the Azure resource provider namespace and resource type of an Azure DocumentDB cluster?
answers.answer: Resource provider namespace: Microsoft.DocumentDB. Primary resource type: Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts (the Cosmos DB account resource).

answers.question: Which Azure CLI command group creates and manages a cluster? Is it in the core CLI or an extension?
answers.answer: Azure CLI group: az cosmosdb (commands like az cosmosdb create, az cosmosdb show, az cosmosdb keys list). This is part of the Azure CLI command set (provided via the azure-cli's cosmosdb command group; no separate third-party extension required for basic account management).

answers.question: Which Bicep and Terraform resource types deploy a cluster?
answers.answer: Bicep / ARM: resource type Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts (set kind or properties to the MongoDB API as needed). Terraform (azurerm): azurerm_cosmosdb_account (set kind = "MongoDB" and the appropriate capabilities/offer_type and consistency/geo settings).

answers.question: What does a connection string look like: scheme, host suffix, port, and the options it must carry?
answers.answer: Use standard MongoDB URI forms. Example (SRV): mongodb+srv://<username>:<password>@<account>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com/?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb&retrywrites=false. Example (standard): mongodb://<username>:<password>@<account>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255/?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb&retrywrites=false&maxIdleTimeMS=120000. Username is typically formatted as <dbuser> or <dbuser>@<account> (depending on account); TLS/SSL must be enabled (ssl=true) and retryWrites is usually disabled for Cosmos (retrywrites=false).

answers.question: How is capacity provisioned and billed: request units, compute tiers with vCores, serverless, or something else?
answers.answer: Capacity is billed in Azure Cosmos DB model: provisioned throughput in Request Units (RU/s) (manual or autoscale) or serverless (pay-per-request) where supported. There is not a direct vCore-based compute tier for the MongoDB API — billing is RU-based or serverless rather than vCore-based instances.

answers.question: Which authentication methods are supported, and how does a driver authenticate with Microsoft Entra ID?
answers.answer: For the MongoDB API you authenticate with standard MongoDB username/password credentials (the Cosmos DB account keys or database users created for the account) using the MongoDB SCRAM mechanism. Microsoft Entra ID (Azure AD) integrated authentication is not generally supported for the MongoDB API data-plane (so you cannot normally use Azure AD token-based auth from a regular MongoDB driver).

answers.question: Which client library should an application use? Is there a service-specific SDK?
answers.answer: Use the standard MongoDB drivers for your language (e.g., pymongo for Python). There is also the Azure Cosmos DB SDK (azure-cosmos) but for the MongoDB-compatible API you should use the regular MongoDB driver rather than the service-specific SDK.

answers.question: Which vector index types are supported, and what does the command that creates one look like?
answers.answer: Azure Cosmos DB (MongoDB API / DocumentDB) does not provide native vector indexes (IVF, HNSW, etc.) as a built-in index type. There is no MongoDB-style command to create a vector-ivf index in Cosmos DB. You must store vectors as data and perform vector search in-app or via an external vector search service (Azure Cognitive Search or a dedicated vector DB).

answers.question: How are full-text search and hybrid search done?
answers.answer: Full-text / hybrid search is not provided as a native MongoDB text index feature in Cosmos DB; the recommended approach is to index Cosmos DB documents into Azure Cognitive Search (Azure Search) and run full-text / hybrid queries there. Alternatively, use an external search/vector engine or bring-your-own search solution.

answers.question: Which MongoDB wire protocol or server versions are supported, and which commonly used MongoDB features are not?
answers.answer: Compatibility is provided to specific MongoDB server versions depending on the account configuration (historically 3.2/3.6/4.0/4.2 and later added compat for newer versions). Exact supported server-version compatibility depends on the selected API/compatibility level of the account. Commonly unsupported or partially supported features include some server-side JavaScript, certain aggregation stages/operators, and historically some newer MongoDB-only features (and change streams / advanced replica-set behavior) have been unavailable or limited. Test against the account's advertised MongoDB version for exact behavior.

answers.question: How do you run the database locally for development and tests: which image or emulator, and which port?
answers.answer: There is no local emulator that fully supports the Cosmos DB MongoDB API. For local development, run a local MongoDB instance (Docker image mongo:latest) and use the standard MongoDB port 27017. Do not expect the Cosmos-specific compatibility quirks to appear locally — test against a real Cosmos DB account for full validation.

answers.question: Are change streams supported, and does anything have to be enabled first?
answers.answer: Change streams are generally not supported on older MongoDB-compatibility levels of Cosmos DB; support depends on the MongoDB server version compatibility that the Cosmos account exposes. In many Cosmos DB MongoDB API accounts change streams were not available. If you need change-stream-like behavior, you must check the account's supported features or use alternative approaches (Azure Functions + Cosmos DB Change Feed for the SQL/Core API).

answers.question: Which MCP server gives an agent data-plane tools for this service? Does the general Azure MCP Server cover it?
answers.answer: There is no special separate MCP server solely for Cosmos DB/MongoDB API; the general Azure management/control plane is used. Data-plane agent tooling (monitoring, diagnostics) is provided via Azure Monitor / Diagnostics and the general Azure agent infrastructure. There is no distinct, separate MCP server you must deploy for basic data-plane access.

answers.question: What was this service called before, and how does it relate to Azure Cosmos DB and to the open-source DocumentDB project?
answers.answer: Historically Microsoft marketed a service called DocumentDB which was the precursor to Azure Cosmos DB's SQL API; Azure DocumentDB references that lineage. Azure Cosmos DB is the superset platform; the MongoDB-compatible offering is Cosmos DB's MongoDB API. The open-source "DocumentDB" project (if referenced elsewhere) is unrelated — Azure DocumentDB was Microsoft’s hosted document database that evolved into Cosmos DB.

answers.question: What engine is underneath, and does that change anything in application code?
answers.answer: Underneath is the Azure Cosmos DB engine exposing a MongoDB wire-protocol compatibility layer. Application code using standard MongoDB drivers will work in most cases, but some MongoDB server behaviors or newer features might be absent or behave differently, so you must validate queries, aggregations, transactions and indexes against Cosmos DB's MongoDB compatibility level.

answers.question: Which Python client library will I use to talk to the MongoDB-compatible DocumentDB account for this sample app?
answers.answer: Use the standard pymongo MongoClient (pymongo). Example: from pymongo import MongoClient; client = MongoClient("mongodb://<username>:<password>@<account>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255/?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb&retrywrites=false").

answers.question: How should vectors be stored in DocumentDB as BSON binary in Python?
answers.answer: Store vectors as BSON binary using bson.binary.Binary. Example: from bson.binary import Binary; doc['embedding'] = Binary(struct.pack('<{}f'.format(len(vec)), *vec)) — store raw float32 bytes or a JSON array. Cosmos DB will store the binary blob but has no native vector type.

answers.question: What index creation command will I run in DocumentDB to create a vector-ivf index for fast ANN search?
answers.answer: You cannot create a native vector-ivf index in Azure Cosmos DB's MongoDB API — there is no supported command to create IVF/HNSW vector indexes. The sample must either (a) do client-side brute-force nearest-neighbor on stored vectors, or (b) push vectors into an external vector search service (Azure Cognitive Search with custom pipeline or a dedicated vector DB).

answers.question: What concrete connection string will I use in code to connect pymongo to a Cosmos DB MongoDB API account?
answers.answer: Example connection string to use in code: mongodb://<username>:<password>@<account>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255/?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb&retrywrites=false&maxIdleTimeMS=120000 — pass this into pymongo.MongoClient(...) for TLS-secured connections.

answers.question: Can I authenticate my Python app to DocumentDB using Microsoft Entra (Azure AD) tokens with the pymongo driver?
answers.answer: No — for the MongoDB-compatible API you should plan to authenticate with the Cosmos DB/MongoDB username and password (account keys or database users). Azure AD token-based auth is not generally available for the MongoDB API data plane, so use connection strings with the account credentials.
